raw_evidence.label: Origin: The Pudding 'Are Men Singing Higher in Pop Music?' (Aug 2019)
raw_evidence.content: This dataset accompanies The Pudding's August 2019 essay 'Are Men Singing Higher in Pop Music?' by Matt Daniels. The piece used Pandora's vocal-register score — a 1-to-10 scale produced by the Music Genome Project's musicologists — joined to roughly 60 years of Billboard Hot 100 chart data (1958-2019). The published archive contains four CSVs: songs.csv (one row per Hot 100 song with male vocals, 1958-2019, n=11,944), 2019.csv (the 248 charting songs from 2019 narrowed to 80 male-led tracks, with gender, genre, and a 'spoken' flag for rap/hip-hop), avg.csv (yearly mean register across all charting male-led songs), and avg_top.csv (yearly mean register restricted to top-10 hits). Daniels worked with Estelle Caswell at Vox's Earworm series, whose companion video 'We Measured Pop Music's Falsetto Obsession' aired the same month and reached the Webby Awards.

raw_evidence.label: Headline finding: 2019 top-10 register hit a 60-year high
raw_evidence.content: Daniels's central claim is that, looking only at top-10 Billboard hits with male vocal leads, 2019 was the highest-register year in the dataset's 60-year window. Four of the five top-10 male-led hits that year sat in high register, including Khalid's 'Talk' (which peaked at #3 on the Hot 100 and ranked #8 on Billboard's 2019 year-end chart). The all-songs average for 2019 was 5.95, lower than the '70s and '80s peaks; the top-10 average tells a different story — the very biggest songs are now sung high, even though the average male-led charting song is not particularly high. The previous register peak in the all-songs series was 1988 (Guns N' Roses, Aerosmith, Poison, hair-metal high belts). Another high earlier era was 1977-78, the Saturday Night Fever years, anchored by the Bee Gees' falsetto-led 'Stayin' Alive' (#1 for four weeks).

raw_evidence.label: The 2019 top/all gap (1.65) is the largest in 60 years
raw_evidence.content: In a typical year, the average register of the top-10 male-led songs sits around 0.3-0.5 points above the average for all male-led charting songs. In 2019, that gap explodes to 1.65 — top-10 at 7.60 minus all-songs at 5.95. This is more than double the next-largest gap on record (0.78 in 2015) and a complete inversion of 1995, the only year where top-10 actually averaged below the all-songs mean (a gap of -0.25). Translation: in 2019, hitting the top 10 with a male voice required singing higher than almost any other path to the chart.
raw_evidence.code:
combined = avg_sorted.merge(top_sorted, on='year', suffixes=('_all', '_top10'))
combined['gap'] = combined['avg_top10'] - combined['avg_all']
print(combined.tail(10))
print("max gap:", combined.loc[combined['gap'].idxmax()].to_dict())
print("min gap (most negative):", combined.loc[combined['gap'].idxmin()].to_dict())
print("2019 gap:", combined[combined['year']==2019].iloc[0].to_dict())

raw_evidence.label: Origin: The Pudding 'Are Men Singing Higher in Pop Music?' (Aug 2019)
raw_evidence.content: This dataset accompanies The Pudding's August 2019 essay 'Are Men Singing Higher in Pop Music?' by Matt Daniels. The piece used Pandora's vocal-register score — a 1-to-10 scale produced by the Music Genome Project's musicologists — joined to roughly 60 years of Billboard Hot 100 chart data (1958-2019). The published archive contains four CSVs: songs.csv (one row per Hot 100 song with male vocals, 1958-2019, n=11,944), 2019.csv (the 248 charting songs from 2019 narrowed to 80 male-led tracks, with gender, genre, and a 'spoken' flag for rap/hip-hop), avg.csv (yearly mean register across all charting male-led songs), and avg_top.csv (yearly mean register restricted to top-10 hits). Daniels worked with Estelle Caswell at Vox's Earworm series, whose companion video 'We Measured Pop Music's Falsetto Obsession' aired the same month and reached the Webby Awards.

raw_evidence.label: The 2019 top/all gap (1.65) is the largest in 60 years
raw_evidence.content: In a typical year, the average register of the top-10 male-led songs sits around 0.3-0.5 points above the average for all male-led charting songs. In 2019, that gap explodes to 1.65 — top-10 at 7.60 minus all-songs at 5.95. This is more than double the next-largest gap on record (0.78 in 2015) and a complete inversion of 1995, the only year where top-10 actually averaged below the all-songs mean (a gap of -0.25). Translation: in 2019, hitting the top 10 with a male voice required singing higher than almost any other path to the chart.

raw_evidence.label: How Pandora's vocal-register score is built
raw_evidence.content: Pandora's Music Genome Project codes each song along ~450 attributes that human musicologists score after listening for 20-30 minutes. Vocal characteristics include the lead vocalist's gender, timbre, breathiness, gruffness, and whether the voice sits in a high or low register. The 'register' value used in this dataset is one of those attributes — a hand-coded 1-to-10 scale where 1 is a deep chest voice (Daniels cites Barry White-style examples as roughly a 2) and 10 is a near-the-top performance like Ginuwine's 'Pony', which scored a 10/10. The scale collapses head voice and chest voice into a single perceived-pitch axis; it does not directly measure falsetto, which is a vocal mechanism rather than a pitch height. That distinction matters: a song can be high in register without being falsetto, and a falsetto passage can sit in a moderate register if it follows a higher belted passage.

raw_evidence.label: Falsetto vs. register: why the distinction matters
raw_evidence.content: Falsetto is a vocal mechanism produced by vibration of the ligamentous edges of the vocal folds, sitting just above the modal (chest) register and overlapping with it by roughly an octave. Male singers historically used falsetto for high notes, while women generally use head voice. The technique was foundational before women sang in choirs and was revived in 20th-century pop by Smokey Robinson, Frankie Valli, the Bee Gees, Prince, and many others. By the late 2010s, critics noted falsetto had become a clear trend among male pop stars including Justin Bieber, The Weeknd, Bruno Mars, Drake, Charlie Puth, Shawn Mendes, Adam Levine, and Sam Smith. In the dataset, however, 'register' is a perceived-height score, so a high register reading captures both high belts and falsetto without separating them.

raw_evidence.label: Falsetto vs. register: why the distinction matters
raw_evidence.content: Falsetto is a vocal mechanism produced by vibration of the ligamentous edges of the vocal folds, sitting just above the modal (chest) register and overlapping with it by roughly an octave. Male singers historically used falsetto for high notes, while women generally use head voice. The technique was foundational before women sang in choirs and was revived in 20th-century pop by Smokey Robinson, Frankie Valli, the Bee Gees, Prince, and many others. By the late 2010s, critics noted falsetto had become a clear trend among male pop stars including Justin Bieber, The Weeknd, Bruno Mars, Drake, Charlie Puth, Shawn Mendes, Adam Levine, and Sam Smith. In the dataset, however, 'register' is a perceived-height score, so a high register reading captures both high belts and falsetto without separating them.

raw_evidence.label: Full register distribution across 11,944 songs
raw_evidence.content: The full distribution of register values across all 11,944 male-led Hot 100 songs from 1958-2019 is single-peaked at 7 (27.7%, 3,310 songs), with 6 (21.4%) and 5 (19.7%) close behind. Only 0.2% of songs (29) score a 2 and only 1.3% (157) score a 10. The most extreme registers are rare — register-9-or-10 covers just 5.0% of the dataset. The bulk of male pop sits at registers 5, 6, 7 — middle-to-moderately-high, what most listeners would call a comfortable tenor.

raw_evidence.label: How Pandora's vocal-register score is built
raw_evidence.content: Pandora's Music Genome Project codes each song along ~450 attributes that human musicologists score after listening for 20-30 minutes. Vocal characteristics include the lead vocalist's gender, timbre, breathiness, gruffness, and whether the voice sits in a high or low register. The 'register' value used in this dataset is one of those attributes — a hand-coded 1-to-10 scale where 1 is a deep chest voice (Daniels cites Barry White-style examples as roughly a 2) and 10 is a near-the-top performance like Ginuwine's 'Pony', which scored a 10/10. The scale collapses head voice and chest voice into a single perceived-pitch axis; it does not directly measure falsetto, which is a vocal mechanism rather than a pitch height. That distinction matters: a song can be high in register without being falsetto, and a falsetto passage can sit in a moderate register if it follows a higher belted passage.

raw_evidence.label: Headline finding: 2019 top-10 register hit a 60-year high
raw_evidence.content: Daniels's central claim is that, looking only at top-10 Billboard hits with male vocal leads, 2019 was the highest-register year in the dataset's 60-year window. Four of the five top-10 male-led hits that year sat in high register, including Khalid's 'Talk' (which peaked at #3 on the Hot 100 and ranked #8 on Billboard's 2019 year-end chart). The all-songs average for 2019 was 5.95, lower than the '70s and '80s peaks; the top-10 average tells a different story — the very biggest songs are now sung high, even though the average male-led charting song is not particularly high. The previous register peak in the all-songs series was 1988 (Guns N' Roses, Aerosmith, Poison, hair-metal high belts). Another high earlier era was 1977-78, the Saturday Night Fever years, anchored by the Bee Gees' falsetto-led 'Stayin' Alive' (#1 for four weeks).

raw_evidence.label: Benchmarks for context
raw_evidence.content: Useful external benchmarks the analyst should keep at hand. The 1-10 scale's anchors as Daniels uses them: ~2 = baritone belt or croon (e.g., Barry White), ~5 = mid-range tenor (most baseline pop), ~7 = noticeably high belt, 10 = near-the-ceiling delivery (Ginuwine's 'Pony'). Billboard Hot 100 has been the canonical US singles chart since 1958, so the dataset's first year (1958) is the chart's first year. Saturday Night Fever's release at the end of 1977 produced one of the genre's most famous mass-market falsetto eras, and 'Stayin' Alive' staying at #1 for four weeks in early 1978 is a useful real-world anchor for what a high-register-dominant year sounds like.

raw_evidence.label: 1990 was the all-time all-songs register peak (7.08)
raw_evidence.content: Sorted by all-songs mean register, the dataset's top decade by far is 1979-1991 — twelve consecutive years of mean register at 6.86 or higher. 1990 (7.0807) edges out 1987 (7.0802) and 1988 (7.0782) for the all-time peak. By 1992 the average drops to 6.48 and never recovers past 6.40 again. This is the unambiguous baseline against which the modern top-10 spike must be read.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmarks for context
raw_evidence.content: Useful external benchmarks the analyst should keep at hand. The 1-10 scale's anchors as Daniels uses them: ~2 = baritone belt or croon (e.g., Barry White), ~5 = mid-range tenor (most baseline pop), ~7 = noticeably high belt, 10 = near-the-ceiling delivery (Ginuwine's 'Pony'). Billboard Hot 100 has been the canonical US singles chart since 1958, so the dataset's first year (1958) is the chart's first year. Saturday Night Fever's release at the end of 1977 produced one of the genre's most famous mass-market falsetto eras, and 'Stayin' Alive' staying at #1 for four weeks in early 1978 is a useful real-world anchor for what a high-register-dominant year sounds like.

raw_evidence.label: 1990 was the all-time all-songs register peak (7.08)
raw_evidence.content: Sorted by all-songs mean register, the dataset's top decade by far is 1979-1991 — twelve consecutive years of mean register at 6.86 or higher. 1990 (7.0807) edges out 1987 (7.0802) and 1988 (7.0782) for the all-time peak. By 1992 the average drops to 6.48 and never recovers past 6.40 again. This is the unambiguous baseline against which the modern top-10 spike must be read.

raw_evidence.label: Headline finding: 2019 top-10 register hit a 60-year high
raw_evidence.content: Daniels's central claim is that, looking only at top-10 Billboard hits with male vocal leads, 2019 was the highest-register year in the dataset's 60-year window. Four of the five top-10 male-led hits that year sat in high register, including Khalid's 'Talk' (which peaked at #3 on the Hot 100 and ranked #8 on Billboard's 2019 year-end chart). The all-songs average for 2019 was 5.95, lower than the '70s and '80s peaks; the top-10 average tells a different story — the very biggest songs are now sung high, even though the average male-led charting song is not particularly high. The previous register peak in the all-songs series was 1988 (Guns N' Roses, Aerosmith, Poison, hair-metal high belts). Another high earlier era was 1977-78, the Saturday Night Fever years, anchored by the Bee Gees' falsetto-led 'Stayin' Alive' (#1 for four weeks).

raw_evidence.label: 1980s share of high-register songs (>=8): 30-40%
raw_evidence.content: The 1980s' high-register dominance shows up at the song level too. From 1979 through 1991, the share of charting male-led songs with register 8 or higher sits in a 31-40% band every single year — peaking at 40.2% in 1988. By contrast, in 2017 only 5.8% of charting male-led songs scored 8 or higher (the lowest in the dataset), and 2019 had 16.2%. The 1980s peak was a high-register monoculture in a way 2019 is not.

Four of the five top-10 male-led hits that year sat in high register, including Khalid's 'Talk' (which peaked at #3 on the Hot 100 and ranked #8 on Billboard's 2019 year-end chart). The all-songs average for 2019 was 5.95, lower than the '70s and '80s peaks; the top-10 average tells a different story — the very biggest songs are now sung high, even though the average male-led charting song is not particularly high. The previous register peak in the all-songs series was 1988 (Guns N' Roses, Aerosmith, Poison, hair-metal high belts). Another high earlier era was 1977-78, the Saturday Night Fever years, anchored by the Bee Gees' falsetto-led 'Stayin' Alive' (#1 for four weeks).

raw_evidence.label: Benchmarks for context
raw_evidence.content: Useful external benchmarks the analyst should keep at hand. The 1-10 scale's anchors as Daniels uses them: ~2 = baritone belt or croon (e.g., Barry White), ~5 = mid-range tenor (most baseline pop), ~7 = noticeably high belt, 10 = near-the-ceiling delivery (Ginuwine's 'Pony'). Billboard Hot 100 has been the canonical US singles chart since 1958, so the dataset's first year (1958) is the chart's first year. Saturday Night Fever's release at the end of 1977 produced one of the genre's most famous mass-market falsetto eras, and 'Stayin' Alive' staying at #1 for four weeks in early 1978 is a useful real-world anchor for what a high-register-dominant year sounds like.

raw_evidence.label: 1980s share of high-register songs (>=8): 30-40%
raw_evidence.content: The 1980s' high-register dominance shows up at the song level too. From 1979 through 1991, the share of charting male-led songs with register 8 or higher sits in a 31-40% band every single year — peaking at 40.2% in 1988. By contrast, in 2017 only 5.8% of charting male-led songs scored 8 or higher (the lowest in the dataset), and 2019 had 16.2%. The 1980s peak was a high-register monoculture in a way 2019 is not.

raw_evidence.label: Why a reader should care: the radio sound of the 2010s changed
raw_evidence.content: The dataset matters because it makes audible something most listeners felt but rarely measured: by the late 2010s the dominant texture of a hit pop song with a male voice had shifted from belted chest-voice rock or croon-style baritone toward a softer, higher, often-falsetto delivery. The Vox Earworm video built on Daniels's data argues that male falsetto became 'nearly impossible to turn on the radio and not hear', tying the trend to streaming-era pop, the rise of the bedroom-pop and post-Drake R&B aesthetic, and EDM's preference for high vocal hooks layered over electronic beats. Independent of cause, the rendering of the chart year by year is the cleanest available picture of a stylistic shift that shaped a decade of radio.

raw_evidence.label: Headline finding: 2019 top-10 register hit a 60-year high
raw_evidence.content: Daniels's central claim is that, looking only at top-10 Billboard hits with male vocal leads, 2019 was the highest-register year in the dataset's 60-year window. Four of the five top-10 male-led hits that year sat in high register, including Khalid's 'Talk' (which peaked at #3 on the Hot 100 and ranked #8 on Billboard's 2019 year-end chart). The all-songs average for 2019 was 5.95, lower than the '70s and '80s peaks; the top-10 average tells a different story — the very biggest songs are now sung high, even though the average male-led charting song is not particularly high. The previous register peak in the all-songs series was 1988 (Guns N' Roses, Aerosmith, Poison, hair-metal high belts). Another high earlier era was 1977-78, the Saturday Night Fever years, anchored by the Bee Gees' falsetto-led 'Stayin' Alive' (#1 for four weeks).

raw_evidence.label: The 2019 top/all gap (1.65) is the largest in 60 years
raw_evidence.content: In a typical year, the average register of the top-10 male-led songs sits around 0.3-0.5 points above the average for all male-led charting songs. In 2019, that gap explodes to 1.65 — top-10 at 7.60 minus all-songs at 5.95. This is more than double the next-largest gap on record (0.78 in 2015) and a complete inversion of 1995, the only year where top-10 actually averaged below the all-songs mean (a gap of -0.25). Translation: in 2019, hitting the top 10 with a male voice required singing higher than almost any other path to the chart.

raw_evidence.label: Headline finding: 2019 top-10 register hit a 60-year high
raw_evidence.content: Daniels's central claim is that, looking only at top-10 Billboard hits with male vocal leads, 2019 was the highest-register year in the dataset's 60-year window. Four of the five top-10 male-led hits that year sat in high register, including Khalid's 'Talk' (which peaked at #3 on the Hot 100 and ranked #8 on Billboard's 2019 year-end chart). The all-songs average for 2019 was 5.95, lower than the '70s and '80s peaks; the top-10 average tells a different story — the very biggest songs are now sung high, even though the average male-led charting song is not particularly high. The previous register peak in the all-songs series was 1988 (Guns N' Roses, Aerosmith, Poison, hair-metal high belts). Another high earlier era was 1977-78, the Saturday Night Fever years, anchored by the Bee Gees' falsetto-led 'Stayin' Alive' (#1 for four weeks).

raw_evidence.label: The 2019 top/all gap (1.65) is the largest in 60 years
raw_evidence.content: In a typical year, the average register of the top-10 male-led songs sits around 0.3-0.5 points above the average for all male-led charting songs. In 2019, that gap explodes to 1.65 — top-10 at 7.60 minus all-songs at 5.95. This is more than double the next-largest gap on record (0.78 in 2015) and a complete inversion of 1995, the only year where top-10 actually averaged below the all-songs mean (a gap of -0.25). Translation: in 2019, hitting the top 10 with a male voice required singing higher than almost any other path to the chart.
raw_evidence.code:
combined = avg_sorted.merge(top_sorted, on='year', suffixes=('_all', '_top10'))
combined['gap'] = combined['avg_top10'] - combined['avg_all']
print(combined.tail(10))
print("max gap:", combined.loc[combined['gap'].idxmax()].to_dict())
print("min gap (most negative):", combined.loc[combined['gap'].idxmin()].to_dict())
print("2019 gap:", combined[combined['year']==2019].iloc[0].to_dict())

raw_evidence.label: Headline finding: 2019 top-10 register hit a 60-year high
raw_evidence.content: Daniels's central claim is that, looking only at top-10 Billboard hits with male vocal leads, 2019 was the highest-register year in the dataset's 60-year window. Four of the five top-10 male-led hits that year sat in high register, including Khalid's 'Talk' (which peaked at #3 on the Hot 100 and ranked #8 on Billboard's 2019 year-end chart). The all-songs average for 2019 was 5.95, lower than the '70s and '80s peaks; the top-10 average tells a different story — the very biggest songs are now sung high, even though the average male-led charting song is not particularly high. The previous register peak in the all-songs series was 1988 (Guns N' Roses, Aerosmith, Poison, hair-metal high belts). Another high earlier era was 1977-78, the Saturday Night Fever years, anchored by the Bee Gees' falsetto-led 'Stayin' Alive' (#1 for four weeks).

raw_evidence.label: Why a reader should care: the radio sound of the 2010s changed
raw_evidence.content: The dataset matters because it makes audible something most listeners felt but rarely measured: by the late 2010s the dominant texture of a hit pop song with a male voice had shifted from belted chest-voice rock or croon-style baritone toward a softer, higher, often-falsetto delivery. The Vox Earworm video built on Daniels's data argues that male falsetto became 'nearly impossible to turn on the radio and not hear', tying the trend to streaming-era pop, the rise of the bedroom-pop and post-Drake R&B aesthetic, and EDM's preference for high vocal hooks layered over electronic beats. Independent of cause, the rendering of the chart year by year is the cleanest available picture of a stylistic shift that shaped a decade of radio.

raw_evidence.label: The 2019 top/all gap (1.65) is the largest in 60 years
raw_evidence.content: In a typical year, the average register of the top-10 male-led songs sits around 0.3-0.5 points above the average for all male-led charting songs. In 2019, that gap explodes to 1.65 — top-10 at 7.60 minus all-songs at 5.95. This is more than double the next-largest gap on record (0.78 in 2015) and a complete inversion of 1995, the only year where top-10 actually averaged below the all-songs mean (a gap of -0.25). Translation: in 2019, hitting the top 10 with a male voice required singing higher than almost any other path to the chart.

raw_evidence.label: Genre split in 2019: rap pulls register down, ballads push it up
raw_evidence.content: Inside 2019.csv, the genre split is stark. Rap/Hip hop's 108 charting songs average register 4.45 — the lowest of any major genre. R&B (3 songs) averages 7.33. The large 'no genre' bucket (the bucket Pandora uses for songs that don't fit a single label, often pop/dance/electronic crossovers) averages 6.36 and contains nearly all of 2019's high-register songs (24 of the 27 with register>=8). Country averages 5.30, Pop 6.00. The same pattern shows up in the 'spoken' axis: songs that score 0 on the spoken (i.e., fully sung) average 6.31 in register; songs that score 8-10 (rapped) average 4.14.

# --- ana_2019_genre: register by genre in 2019 ---
print("=== ana_2019_genre ===")
# normalize duplicate "no genreno genre"
y2019['genre_clean'] = y2019['genre'].replace({'no genreno genre':'no genre'}).fillna('no genre')
print("genre counts after cleaning:")
print(y2019['genre_clean'].value_counts())
print("register by genre (all):")
print(y2019.groupby('genre_clean')['register'].agg(['count','mean','median','std','min','max']).round(3).sort_values('mean', ascending=False))

# --- ana_2019_spoken: spoken-vocals share and effect ---
# spoken column appears to be 0-10 scale (degree of rapped delivery)
print("=== ana_2019_spoken ===")
print("spoken value counts:")
print(y2019['spoken'].value_counts(dropna=False).sort_index())
# Bucket
y2019['spoken_bucket'] = pd.cut(y2019['spoken'], bins=[-1,0,4,7,10],
                                 labels=['sung (0)','mostly sung (1-4)','mixed (5-7)','rapped (8-10)'])
print("register by spoken bucket:")
print(y2019.groupby('spoken_bucket', observed=False)['register'].agg(['count','mean','median']).round(3))

# --- ana_2019_male_subset: register among male leads (excluding spoken-rap >=8) ---
print("=== ana_2019_male_subset ===")
male_sung = y2019[(y2019['gender']=='male') & (y2019['spoken']<8)]
print("n male, mostly-sung:", len(male_sung))
print("mean register:", round(male_sung['register'].mean(), 3))
print("median:", male_sung['register'].median())
print("Distribution:")
print(male_sung['register'].value_counts().sort_index())
# Compare to female
female = y2019[y2019['gender']=='female']
print("n female:", len(female))
print("female mean register:", round(female['register'].mean(), 3))

# --- ana_2019_high_register: distribution of high-register songs ---
print("=== ana_2019_high_register ===")
hi = y2019[y2019['register'] >= 8]
print(f"songs with register >= 8: {len(hi)} / {len(y2019)} = {len(hi)/len(y2019)*100:.1f}%")
print("by gender:")
print(hi['gender'].value_counts())
print("by genre:")

Source: We measured pop music's falsetto obsession — Vox Earworm (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qJT2h5uGAC0) Facts: Vox Earworm episode released Aug 2019 collaborating with The Pudding; Argues falsetto is 'nearly impossible to turn on the radio and not hear' Source: How EDM Grew Up & Swallowed Pop Music Whole — Feed.fm (https://blog.feed.fm/how-edm-grew-up-swallowed-pop-music-whole-trends-in-electro) Facts: By the late 2010s dance music was the third most popular global genre; Streaming services and EDM cross-pollination reshaped pop production

raw_evidence.label: Why a reader should care: the radio sound of the 2010s changed
raw_evidence.content: The dataset matters because it makes audible something most listeners felt but rarely measured: by the late 2010s the dominant texture of a hit pop song with a male voice had shifted from belted chest-voice rock or croon-style baritone toward a softer, higher, often-falsetto delivery. The Vox Earworm video built on Daniels's data argues that male falsetto became 'nearly impossible to turn on the radio and not hear', tying the trend to streaming-era pop, the rise of the bedroom-pop and post-Drake R&B aesthetic, and EDM's preference for high vocal hooks layered over electronic beats. Independent of cause, the rendering of the chart year by year is the cleanest available picture of a stylistic shift that shaped a decade of radio.

Independent of cause, the rendering of the chart year by year is the cleanest available picture of a stylistic shift that shaped a decade of radio.
